question: Whipple's triad for confirming hypoglycaemia in a clinical setting consists of which three components?

answers.text: Low blood glucose + symptoms + response to glucose administration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Whipple's triad: (1) symptoms consistent with hypoglycaemia, (2) documented low blood glucose at the time of symptoms (<3.9 mmol/L or <70 mg/dL), and (3) relief of symptoms after glucose administration. All three must be present.

answers.text: Blood glucose <70 mg/dL + sweating + loss of consciousness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Loss of consciousness is severe (neuroglycopenic) hypoglycaemia but not a required component of Whipple's triad. Many patients are symptomatic without losing consciousness.
Tremor and palpitations are adrenergic features of hypoglycaemia, but blood glucose <110 mg/dL is not the threshold. The clinical threshold is <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L).

answers.text: Symptoms + insulin administration history + improvement with IV dextrose only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Whipple's triad does not require IV dextrose specifically — any form of glucose (oral or IV) that relieves symptoms satisfies the third criterion. Insulin history is also not part of the triad.

overallFeedback.feedback: Memorise Whipple's triad: (1) symptoms of hypoglycaemia + (2) documented low glucose at the time of symptoms + (3) relief with glucose administration. All three criteria must be met.
Excellent — Whipple's triad is the gold standard for confirming hypoglycaemia regardless of cause.
